options.title: Survey Poisson regression - prevalence ratio
options.when: Cross-sectional studies, especially when the outcome is common (outcome in about 19% of participants)
pros: Directly interpretable as 'x times as common'
Collapsible: unadjusted and adjusted estimates are comparable
Robust (sandwich) variance from the survey design
cons: Less familiar to some readers than odds ratios
Fitted probabilities can exceed 1 (rarely matters for PRs)
options.literature: Used in 2 of 12 similar NHANES papers in high-impact journals

options.title: Prevalence ratio primary, odds ratio as a sensitivity analysis
options.when: You want the better estimand and comparability with the literature
pros: Shows how much the OR exaggerates the PR

options.title: Survey logistic regression - odds ratio
options.when: Rare outcomes (<10%), or when matching the published NHANES literature matters most (outcome in about 19% of participants)
pros: Most widely used model in NHANES papers - easy to compare with prior work
cons: Overstates the prevalence ratio when the outcome is common - here roughly 19%
Non-collapsible: ORs shift with adjustment even without confounding
options.literature: Used in 6 of 12 similar NHANES papers in high-impact journals

options.title: Multiple imputation (chained equations) for missing covariates
options.when: Complete-case loss is 18% in this run
pros: Less bias if data are missing at random
cons: Assumes missing at random given the imputation model
options.literature: Used in 1 of 12 similar NHANES papers in high-impact journals

options.title: Log-binomial regression - risk ratio
options.when: When a reviewer insists on a binomial model
pros: Same estimand as Poisson PR with binomial variance
cons: Often fails to converge with several covariates
Not run by the engine - Poisson PR estimates the same quantity
options.literature: Used in 0 of 12 similar NHANES papers in high-impact journals

rationale: Survey Poisson regression - prevalence ratio scores highest (86/100) for this outcome; used in 2 of 12 similar NHANES papers in high-impact journals. The plan already uses it.
basis: rule-based scoring with methods learned from published papers
